commentary.bottom_line: Thirteen sources endorse multi-site validation, and studies that broke results out by site or device found performance gaps that pooled figures hid. No study compared this practice with pooled validation or measured patient outcomes, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: Of 44 studies listed as testing the practice, most applied a model at several sites or on several devices. None compared per-site reporting with pooled reporting or tracked patient outcomes, and some reported only pooled accuracy. Per-site and per-device breakdowns exposed gaps in several studies, which suggests the practice detects variation. Indirectness and inconsistent reporting lower certainty to low.

Per-device reporting surfaced weaknesses that combined figures concealed. One retinal tool had 97.1% combined sensitivity but 83.3% on ZEISS images, and a pathology model's grading agreement fell to 0.44 on one scanner. In hazard studies, sepsis AUROC fell from 0.92 at development to 0.77 externally, and coding precision fell from 0.875 to 0.137.

A qualitative study of 39 interviews linked site variation to workflow integration, technical configuration, and infrastructure, which a one-time validation may not capture. In a smartphone study, image capture succeeded in 28.9% of attempts in users' hands, and diagnostic performance differed by phone model. Device-level validation may need to use the equipment that staff and patients actually use.

In a tuberculosis screening trial in South Africa and Lesotho, staff had to re-determine site thresholds because score distributions depended on each site's X-ray equipment. Per-hospital fine-tuning of a terminology mapping model produced top-1 accuracy from 25.0% to 96.3%. These findings suggest per-site validation may bring recurring recalibration work that budgets should anticipate.

Device-dependent gaps appeared in low-resource settings. In rural India, one diabetic retinopathy tool had 97.5% sensitivity on one camera and 81.7% on another. Among the testing studies, one used an Iraqi cohort, and none enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software says multiple collection sites, such as academic and community hospitals, may assure a more representative sample. FUTURE-AI advises selecting multiple evaluation sites. The quoted regulatory and consensus passages do not address separate reporting by site or device, so that element rests mainly on commentaries.

Patients usually cannot learn whether a tool was checked on the scanner or phone used in their care. A gestational age study reported error separately for Chicago (4.1 days) and Nairobi (4.3 days). Its reporting shows that site-level results can be stated in terms a clinician could explain to a patient.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared validation with separate site and device reporting against pooled validation for detecting failures before deployment, or linked either approach to patient outcomes. The evidence also does not show how many sites or devices are enough, or what response after a detected gap, such as recalibration or local thresholds, restores performance.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the 44 studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One testing study used an Iraqi cohort and one studied older adults. Hazard studies from rural India, South Africa and Lesotho, and a rural China trial that enrolled limited English proficiency and low-literacy participants documented site- and setting-dependent problems, including consultation completion that fell to 40% in mountainous regions (pmid:41659358). Health systems serving these populations probably cannot assume that validation at other sites will transfer, and local validation may be needed.
